In the seminar room of the physics department, Pankaj, a first-year, raised a point about the experiment. "The readings drift because of the temperature, so if we..."
"Yes, and we can just repeat it," said Jahnavi, a final-year student, cutting in. Others nodded. Ten minutes later Jahnavi said, "My idea is to control the temperature," and the professor wrote it down.
Pankaj felt hot, then went quiet and looked at the notes. After the session, Pankaj walked up. "Jahnavi, I said the temperature part earlier, and I was cut off. I'd like to finish my thought next time." Jahnavi paused. "You did. I'm sorry."

qa.q: What did Jahnavi say ten minutes later that the professor wrote down?
qa.a: Jahnavi said, "My idea is to control the temperature."

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling after the idea was credited to Jahnavi?
qa.a: Pankaj felt hurt and unheard, going hot and then quiet. Looking at the notes shows a wish to disappear from the discussion.

qa.q: What did Pankaj do after the session, and how did it help?
qa.a: Pankaj walked up and said the temperature point was Pankaj's and had been cut off, and asked to finish next time. Jahnavi paused, apologised and acknowledged it.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt when Pankaj spoke after the session?
qa.a: Jahnavi was probably caught off guard, but then acknowledged the mistake and apologised. The calm request made it easy to accept.

grounding: A student whose points are cut off and later credited to a senior goes quiet, then asks to finish the thought.

passage:
Subject: Finishing my point in group meetings
Dear Gurleen,
I hope you are well. In Tuesday's project meeting I began to explain the survey design, but was interrupted twice, and later the same idea was presented as Rohan's. I stayed quiet, and I think I have been quiet in the last few meetings too.
I'd like to ask a small thing: could we agree that each person finishes their point before someone else answers? I am happy to write my ideas in the shared document too, so they are on record.
Thank you for listening. I would like the group to work well.
Best,
Sarika

qa.q: On which day was the project meeting where Sarika was interrupted?
qa.a: The project meeting was on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when staying quiet in the meeting?
qa.a: Sarika was hurt and discouraged, feeling unheard after the idea was credited to someone else. The email admits going quiet in later meetings too.

qa.q: What did Sarika ask for in the email, and why is it a good approach?
qa.a: Sarika asked that each person finish a point before someone else answers, and offered to put ideas in the shared document. It is polite, specific and practical.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see Sarika's email?
qa.a: Gurleen may be surprised but can see a clear, calm request and a wish for the group to work well. The tone makes it easy to agree.

grounding: A student whose points are repeatedly cut off and credited to someone else goes quiet, then emails to ask to finish the thought.
